TEXT:
NDIS revolving door heavenly for recruiter Russell Reynolds

The National Disability Insurance Agency made its 2018-19 annual report public on Wednesday.

It was a cycle of tumult and turnover at the agency's top echelon, with chief executive Rob de Luca abruptly pulling stumps in April. So only naturally, we turned straight to Appendix E: Executive remuneration, the first year that board and key management personnel compensation has been broken out.

Before quitting with immediate effect and joining disability care provider Zenitas, de Luca was drawing an annual salary of $704,689. One of de Luca's deputies Vicki Rundle became acting CEO (where she remains) on April 30. She was paid $432,168 for the year.

And despite her seniority during two months of higher duties, Rundle was out-earned by her fellow deputy CEO Michael Francis ($453,451), who resigned in July and finished last month; and by Head of Markets Antonia Albanese ($460,120), who joined de Luca at Zenitas in July; and even by her Head of People Hamish Aikman, who took home $481,281. For human resources! If ever an organisational function was ripe for automation ...

But she wasn't out-earned by the other deputy CEO Anthony Vella ($427,715), who quit in July and joined de Luca in August.

Yep, four of the NDIA's eight most senior executives - the CEO included - have left in six months flat. Chaos. What kind of show is chairman Helen Nugent ($158,801) running here?!

There's one mob never happier than when pumping the motor on a revolving door, and that's executive recruiters Russell Reynolds. The Department of Social Services engaged the search firm (through a limited tender) to identify new NDIA directors in 2015, but the Abbott government's mooted "shake-up" of the board ultimately petered into a gentler regeneration, in January 2017. Russell Reynolds then conducted the CEO search that led to de Luca's appointment in July 2017. That contract was awarded without a competitive tender.

Remarkably, given its candidate lasted only 20 months, Russell Reynolds is now engaged by the NDIA board finding to find de Luca's replacement. And given his skimpy tenure, did RR refund - or offer to refund - its fee (money for jam at 20 per cent of the first year's remuneration)? Yeah right!

The NDIA also used Russell Reynolds in 2017 to place Rundle, Francis and chief financial officer Victor Walter, in 2018 to place Aikman, and now to find a successor for Francis (again: two fees, one job).

According to an NDIA spokesperson, all of these search mandates bar Francis Mark II were handed to Russell Reynolds after a competitive process. Must be a killer pitch they've got 'cos boy are they on a winning streak.

It's not exactly the $25 million McKinsey trousered for their usual templated shtick, but these are still handsome fees - and with apparently no economic downside for unearthing misaligned talent. NDIS participants and their families can at least be thankful that the quality of the scheme's care is vastly superior to the quality of its management. Anything would be.

Australia's most complex exports not counted by Harvard boffins

What's the difference between Namibia and Australia? Very little, if you believe the Harvard boffins behind the much-discussed Atlas of Economic Complexity. They reckon Australia's major exports of ores and oil are so unconducive to long-term economic development we might as well be a country peopled by barely educated subsistence farmers.

If a piece of academic research comes up with conclusions as counter-intuitive as this, it should be vigorously examined for methodology flaws. But not, it seems, in Australia, for all its challenges a very wealthy nation so used to debasing itself we'd more easily countenance our future among the world's poorest.

Aside from this newspaper, which both broke news of and reported some scepticism about the survey, gullible reporting of Harvard's research was repeated far and wide in outlets as unfamiliar with matters of economic complexity as SBS' The Feed and the Daily Mail.

But here's something that might explain Australia's position at the bottom of Harvard's league tables. Some of its biggest and most sophisticated exports aren't counted. At all.

The data in Harvard's survey comes from that reported by customs agencies. Service exports don't go through customs offices, and aren't uniformly reported to the United Nations. For the purposes of statistical coherence, trade in services is thus utterly excised.

This is described as an "important drawback" in the book through which Harvard economist Ricardo Hausmann describes his methodology: "Services are becoming a rising share of international trade. Unfortunately, the statistical efforts of most countries of the world have not kept up with this reality".

But if you want a gauge on the character and complexity of the Australian economy, you'd be a fool to leave them out. Services are responsible for 70 per cent of it. That fed through to 22.4 per cent of exports in 2018 and almost double that on a value-added basis. Key contributors were complex fields such as education, telecommunications and financial services.

So, the difference between Australia and Namibia? You could start there.

Fahour's bad luck rubbed off on Gerry Harvey

Did someone place a hex on Gerry Harvey and Ahmed Fahour as they shared a stage in western Sydney to launch Latitude's buy-now, pay-later ambitions a little over a month ago?

How else to explain the fact that within 24 hours of each other, both had failed to convince investors to stump up the cash to invest in their respective businesses.

The failure of the $1 billion float of Fahour's Latitude Financial Group occurred despite Latitude's owners being, in the end, willing to sell stock 11 per cent beneath the bottom of their $2 to $2.25 initial pricing band (and after its joint lead managers sent messages to would-be investors saying demand for the stock "currently exceeds the expected offer size").

Less than a day later, Harvey Norman fell about $8 million short of a $174 million capital-raise, despite its being priced at an extraordinary $2.50 a share, a 46 per cent discount to the trading price.

Seems Harvey Norman shareholders were sceptical of tipping in more cash to fund their own dividends. Meanwhile, others couldn't quite stomach the thought of buying up Latitude (and funding Fahour's $22.5 million pay day).

Still, for sheer capital-raising chutzpah, we suppose Fahour and Harvey do make the best-matched of business partners.

HEADLINE: Building on energy market transition
TEXT:
Soaring power prices have prompted Australian businesses to look for innovative solutions, and one retailer is helping them by opening up access to the wholesale energy market.

Melbourne-based Flow Power has developed a model aimed at providing commercial and industrial users with the same tools that large retailers employ to purchase energy.

These could take the form of large-scale corporate renewables power purchase agreements (PPAs), access to the spot market, use of derivative contracts, and even pricing that allows customers to take advantage of flexible operations.

‘‘What we do is materially very different to what the incumbent players do,’’ says CEO Matthew van der Linden.

‘‘We are very much about delivering results that actually enable customers to unlock value from their energy.’’ While prices constantly change in the wholesale market, they typically stay below the average, which was 8.4c/kWh last calendar year, more than 60 per cent of the time.

New technologies such as renewable energy, are creating opportunities to generate energy at a lower operational cost.

Despite retailers investing heavily in renewables’ capacity in recent years to meet their regulatory obligations, few users have benefited from the falling cost of generation.

One of Flow Power’s key tools to overcome this situation is through corporate renewable PPAs.

Under this arrangement, it contracts power from large-scale wind farms or solar farms and then signs up back-toback long-term contracts with customers for a part of that capacity.

‘‘For a business, it is relatively simple – it’s a significantly reduced cost for their energy by accessing the lower cost renewables,’’ says van der Linden.

‘‘They also achieve sustainability goals and support investment in the new generation.’’ Out of the 76 corporate renewable PPAs publicly announced in Australia, Flow Power has been directly involved in a third.

Some of its major customers include industrial giant Molycop, Sydney Opera House and Olam Orchards.

In October alone, it signed up agreements to move Sydney and Newcastle to 100 per cent renewable energy.

Flow Power employs proprietary energy management technology to help customers manage usage in line with the market.

Its kWatch platform includes a controller and a portal that helps operators spot those times so they can immediately adjust their energy needs.

This could be achieved, for example, by shutting down a crusher at amine or an irrigator’s pumps over short periods of time to minimise exposure to high price peaks.

Alternatively, they can shift to localised power sources such as generators or battery storage, which may be cheaper during such periods. This helps businesses alleviate pressure on the system during peak times.

This is called demand response and customers regularly save up to 30 per cent on their energy costs, with some customers achieving up to 60 per cent savings, the company says.

Flow Power has evolved its offering in the past few years towards thinking holistically about energy – from where it is sourced to how it is used, van der Linden says.

As a result, it has boosted resources in engineering, research and development, behindthe- meter services and account management to ensure it offers a holistic service to energy users.

‘‘We believe technology is crucial for the future so we are dedicating resources to research and development,’’ van der Linden says.

‘‘We are backing that up with a serious engineering department that we have grown in the past 12 months.’’ The retailer now installs a kWatch Controller for every customer signing up to provide live per second usage data, which they say helps businesses manage how they use power.

Flow Power’s growth plans have been supported after one of Canada’s biggest pension funds, OPTrust, acquired majority control in the business last year.

OPTrust has helped Flow Power take on the market in away it couldn’t have previously, van der Linden says, also assisting significantly in securing off-take agreements with projects.

The retailer expects to continue expanding its offerings as it looks to gain share in amarket transitioning to a low-carbon future where renewables are central.

‘‘We are not after just the big players, we really do want to make the corporate PPA model available for everybody,’’ he says.

‘‘Our goal is to continue to put the customer at the centre of the energy market where they take control of their energy needs.’’

HEADLINE: Lowe searches for inflation breathing room
TEXT:
If Australia treated inflation the way the similar economies of Canada and Norway did, the Reserve Bank might not have had to cut interest rates three times this year.

That's the view of economists who fear Reserve Bank governor Philip Lowe has been under pressure to cut rates simply to see inflation hit its target of between 2 to 3 per cent.

Inflation has missed that target for 15 quarters. That is likely to lead to a new agreement between Treasurer Josh Frydenberg and Dr Lowe whereby the central bank has to increase its level of accountability around why the inflation target has been missed.

Dr Lowe said on Tuesday that lower inflation was helping Australians more than hindering them and the flexibility around hitting the inflation target was going to be used by the central bank.

"Conventional wisdom has been that the best contribution a central bank can make to full employment and economic welfare is to maintain low and stable inflation," he said.

"There is an acceptable degree of variation in inflation from year to year, and we have been prepared to use this flexibility. I also want to emphasise that the flexibility of our inflation target and our broad mandate - and the discretion it allows - requires a high level of transparency and accountability from us."

However Warren Hogan, an independent economist and adjunct professor at UTS Business School, said: "We would definitely not have had to cut if the inflation target was between 1 and 3 per cent instead of 2 to 3 per cent. The two most similar economies to ours - Canada and Norway - both have 1 to 3 per cent target bands. This has been much more consistent with global inflation and yet provides the flexibility as well."

QIC chief economist Matthew Peter said the central bank's original mandate to achieve the inflation target was protected by independence.

"In the 1980s, they had a mandate from the government to tackle inflation even though it meant you were going to slow the economy down.

"It was important they had the independence because they were going to make decisions that weren't positive in other aspects of the economy. I don't see it's any difference today."

On Tuesday Dr Lowe said his board had considered how persistently low inflation could hurt people.

"It is possible that, in some circumstances, a low and stable inflation environment provides fertile ground for the emergence of some financial stability risks.

"As we have seen too often, the crystallisation of these risks can have very large welfare consequences, with people losing their jobs, their incomes and their savings."

But Westpac's Bill Evans said the key issue for Dr Lowe was people's expectations. "What they don't want is inflation expectations to fall," he said.

HEADLINE: Drought hit to force up food prices
TEXT:
Scott Donald is nervous that the drought could mean rising food prices within the next six months at his organic grocery store Wray Organic at Cleveland in Brisbane.

"We haven't seen it just yet but the knock-on effect will come soon," Mr Donald said.

"I have been talking to growers now and they say this season is way down, so high prices will come through next season."

The latest inflation figures show fruit prices fell 3.1 per cent in the September quarter, with vegetable prices down 2.5 per cent.

But overall food prices have risen 0.4 per cent in the quarter and show an annual growth rate at 2.3 per cent - roughly the same pace of growth of wages in Australia.

Mr Donald, who sells everything from organic shampoo to honey, said his suppliers were telling him that the range of products was tightening due to lack of rain.

"Our honey suppliers say that because of the lack of rain the trees aren't flowering, which means the bees don't have anything to make honey, so I think the price will go up."

Australian Food and Grocery Council chief executive Tanya Barden said while the latest inflation readings for food and grocery products were up slightly, they do follow seven years of retail price deflation in the sector.

"This is despite significant increases in the cost of manufacturing through rises in energy prices, regulatory costs, and the impacts of the drought," Ms Barden said.

HEADLINE: Strong REITs power property chiefs' pay
TEXT:
The chief executives of the country's top listed real estate companies bagged a 9 per cent lift in pay in the last financial year, with the sector buoyed by a surge in investment chasing property yields. The average statutory pay was $3.94 million for the property chiefs for the most recent financial year, up from the average in the previous period. This compares with $5.12 million for CEOs across all ASX 100 companies. Goodman Group founder Greg Goodman was the highest earner on $12.8 million by a significant margin. He presided over a total shareholder return of close to 60 per cent at his company.

HEADLINE: ICAC urged to probe planning windfall
TEXT:
The NSW corruption watchdog has been urged to investigate a Sydney council's favourable planning decision for disgraced Chinese billionaire Huang Xiangmo as the Labor mayor defies growing pressure to stand aside.

The Australian Financial Review revealed yesterday that Mr Huang's Yuhu Group stands to rake in a $135 million profit from the redevelopment of Eastwood Plaza, which was put up for sale after final approval was granted in August.

China's Poly Group, an arms maker turned property developer, was in discussion to buy the site but withdrew its offer yesterday due to the controversy surrounding the development. Ryde Council, in Sydney's increasingly built-up north-west, approved the development in May, but its deputy mayor Simon Zhou failed to disclose his $4 million interest in another company owned by Mr Huang's Yuhu Group.

Mr Zhou, who previously worked at the ALP's NSW headquarters, sits as an independent on the council.

He holds the balance of power, a position which ensured Labor's Jerome Laxale was elected mayor.

This is the latest headache for Labor in NSW and its relationship with Mr Huang, who had his Australian permanent residency cancelled last year on the advice of ASIO and is accused of making an illegal $100,000 donation to the ALP in 2015.

Ryde mayor Mr Laxale said the councillors were entitled to refer the Yuhu planning decision to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption. But he remained defiant, saying he would not be stepping aside.

"I will not be bowing to their demands. If they want to refer something to ICAC then good on them ... go for it," he said.

ICAC has just finished six weeks of public hearings into that donation and yesterday was asked by a bloc of Ryde's Liberal, Green and Independent councillors to investigate the Yuhu planning decision.

"I'm appalled by the revelations," said Liberal councillor Trenton Brown.

He has written to the general manager seeking an extraordinary meeting of council to have the matter referred to ICAC and for Mr Laxale and Mr Zhou to stand aside while that process runs its course.

Mr Brown is also seeking to have the planning approval set aside until any ICAC investigation has been completed and to compel council staff to fully co-operate with the corruption watchdog.

He said he would move three motions to that effect at an extraordinary council meeting scheduled for November 12.

"I want to make sure no one can profit from a decision where there may have been wrong-doing," Mr Brown said.

Independent councillor Ray Maggio and the Greens' Christopher Gordon have indicated they will support any referral to ICAC. That would comprise six of 10 votes, as Mr Laxale and Mr Zhou would most likely be unable to participate as the matter concerns them.

NSW Labor leader Jodi McKay cancelled a media event with Mr Laxale yesterday morning, fearing she may be dragged into the controversy.

Mr Laxale said the event had been "postponed". Mr Zhou is overseas. Mr Laxale, Mr Zhou and Mr Huang all attended the NSW Friends of Labor dinner in 2015, above. This led to an illegal $100,000 donation, which is alleged to have been made in cash and delivered by Mr Huang to the ALP's headquarters in an Aldi shopping bag. Mr Huang denies this.

Mr Huang is also fighting the tax office, which is seeking $141 million in unpaid liabilities from the property developer.

Mr Zhou formed part of Ryde Council's oversight for the Yuhu proposal, but absented himself from the critical vote on May 28 citing a "less than significant non-pecuniary interest".

He told council he "knows Mr Huang Xiangmo as a Chinese Community Leader" whose family owned Yuhu Group. Mr Zhou failed to mention he had held a $4 million shareholding in a separate Yuhu company, which owns the $82 million Pymble Corporate Centre - a low-rise office complex on Sydney's north shore.

That shareholding would not have increased in value because of the Eastwood Plaza decision, but his failure to disclose the mutual shareholding with Mr Huang may breach disclosure requirements under the Local Government Act and the Code of Conduct for local councils.

Yesterday, the general manager of Ryde Council, George Dedes, referred this potential breach to the Office of Local Government.

He said this was the "appropriate authority" as the matters raised by the Financial Review related to disclosure of a councillor's pecuniary interests.

Mr Zhou has denied any wrongdoing, saying he was just "quietly doing my job".

The Yuhu motion in May was carried by seven votes to four, as the other independent, Mr Maggio, also gave his support.

That means it would have passed even without Mr Zhou's absence.

Mr Maggio told the Financial Review if Mr Zhou had disclosed his financial links with Mr Huang or Yuhu, he would have voted against the motion.

HEADLINE: Morgan warns: bank 'jihad' will backfire
TEXT:
Former Westpac boss David Morgan said the cumulative impact of current pressures on the major banks - including a "jihad" on mortgage pricing by the competition regulator - has plunged the sector into a crisis that threatens banks' ability to support the economy.

Dr Morgan, who ran Westpac for almost a decade to 2008, said the banks were "completely friendless" and their relationship with Canberra was poor.

He described responsible lending as "wrong-headed legislation", and said the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission's mortgage pricing inquiry "will reveal nothing we don't already know - but it is consistent with a jihad on the back-book which the ACCC have".

With ANZ reporting its full-year results today, which will reveal pressure on revenue, returns, net interest margins and capital levels, Dr Morgan said he expected banks will need to raise fresh capital, reduce dividend payout ratios and cut more staff.

"These are pretty severe cumulative consequences. [Banks] are plainly having a very challenging time," he said.
